title: Habitat-Mediated Spillover Risk of Andes Hantavirus in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus: A Mechanistic Eco-Epidemiological Model

analysis.research_question_and_background: Andes hantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Its maintenance and spillover risk depend on the ecology of its principal reservoir, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, and on environmental changes that alter habitat availability, host abundance, and human–rodent interfaces.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model that couples effective habitat cover to an SIR framework for ANDV transmission in O.
analysis.methods: Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity.
analysis.main_results: We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human–rodent interfaces.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows.

analysis.summary_en: The study developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model to understand how habitat changes affect Andes hantavirus transmission in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus. The model showed that while the basic reproduction number R0 is independent of habitat cover, the effective reproduction number Re(t) and infection burden depend on transient habitat conditions, guiding surveillance and prevention strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantavirus infections represent an expanding global zoonotic threat characterized by high mortality rates and limited therapeutic options. analysis.methods: The study combines classical clinical perspectives with contemporary translational research to analyze hantavirus biology, epidemiology, clinical features, diagnostic strategies, and therapeutic approaches. analysis.main_results: The article provides an updated and integrated overview of hantavirus biology, epidemiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic strategies, and emerging therapeutic approaches. title: A systematic review of ultrasound to predict severe disease in patients with dengue and other viral infections associated with hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.scope_and_question: Viral infections associated with hemorrhagic fevers (VaHFs) cause millions of cases each year across a broad geography with severity ranging from asymptomatic cases to clinical disease with a high case fatality rate.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We conducted a systematic review to assess ultrasound findings in VaHFs and their ability to predict severe disease (PROSPERO CRD42024620862).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Pericardial effusions and several other findings were associated with severe disease.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Important limitations included reliance on a single database and possibility of missing manuscripts from local journals, the small number of publications on non-dengue VaHFs, patient recruitment overwhelmingly from the in-hospital setting at tertiary referral centers during high-transmission periods, high degree of heterogeneity, and bias in the timing domain among the studies on dengue.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: We discuss some virus and organ-specific considerations and conclude with detailed considerations for future research.

analysis.summary_en: Viral infections associated with hemorrhagic fevers (VaHFs) cause millions of cases each year across a broad geography with severity ranging from asymptomatic cases to clinical disease with a high case fatality rate. We conducted a systematic review to assess ultrasound findings in VaHFs and their ability to predict severe disease (PROSPERO CRD42024620862). Pericardial effusions and several other findings were associated with severe disease. Important limitations included reliance on a single database and possibility of missing manuscripts from local journals, the small number of publications on non-dengue VaHFs, patient recruitment overwhelmingly from the in-hospital setting at tertiary referral centers during high-transmission periods, high degree of heterogeneity, and bias in the timing domain among the studies on dengue. We discuss some virus and organ-specific considerations and conclude with detailed considerations for future research.

title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the divergent molecular responses of endothelial cells to New World Andes virus (ANDV) and Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV), addressing the knowledge gap in species-specific disease phenotypes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the integration of time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with ANDV or HTNV.
analysis.methods: Time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics were used to analyze human endothelial cells infected with ANDV or HTNV.
analysis.main_results: ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response early in infection, while HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, leading to visual disruption of cellular actin architecture.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identified species-specific responses in endothelial cells, highlighting the importance of ERBB-family kinases as druggable host targets, and revealed mechanisms relevant to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for hantavirus infections, particularly in understanding the mechanisms underlying different clinical manifestations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of human endothelial cells and does not address the full complexity of hantavirus infection in vivo, which may affect the generalizability of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study compared the molecular responses of human endothelial cells to New World Andes virus (ANDV) and Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV), identifying species-specific mechanisms and potential druggable targets.

title: A multispecies convergence zone: viral diversity and zoonotic spillover potential at Cambodia’s cross-border rodent trade hub

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess zoonotic spillover potential at a cross-border rodent trade hub in Cambodia, highlighting the need for systematic multi-host surveillance in live animal trade interfaces due to their role in increasing pathogen exposure through multispecies aggregation and human-animal contact.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted at a cross-border rodent trade hub in Chrey Thom, Cambodia, from 2015 to 2018, involving 1,005 animals and 342 humans. Specimens were collected from rodents, domestic animals, and humans to evaluate viral diversity and spillover potential.
analysis.methods: The researchers performed repeated cross-sectional surveillance using consensus polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays targeting nine viral families. Zoonotic-exposure questionnaires were administered to community members and febrile hospital patients to gather behavioural and awareness data.
analysis.main_results: Among 2,618 specimens, 15.3% were positive, all from animals, with 12 distinct viruses identified. Rodents and poultry had the highest detection rates, at 34.7% and 33.9%, respectively. Coronaviruses, including an HKU1-like betacoronavirus, predominated in rodents. Seoul virus was detected in Rattus argentiventer, and PREDICT-CoV-100, infectious bronchitis virus, and Newcastle disease virus were found in poultry. Influenza A(H5) was detected in ducks and A(H9) in chickens. No viruses were detected by PCR in humans.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that traded rodents and poultry carry diverse viruses, including Seoul virus, which is relevant to hantavirus research. The study highlights the importance of understanding human-animal contact behaviours and awareness of zoonotic transmission routes in such settings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results support the need for integrated One Health surveillance at wildlife trade interfaces to monitor zoonotic pathogens and assess spillover risks. They also provide a rare pre-COVID baseline for evaluating how evolving trade pathways may influence future spillover potential.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on animal specimens and the absence of human viral detection. Despite these limitations, the evidence is moderate in strength due to the comprehensive surveillance approach and the identification of multiple viruses with potential zoonotic relevance.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated a cross-border rodent trade hub in Cambodia to assess zoonotic spillover potential. It found that rodents and poultry carried a high diversity of viruses, including Seoul virus, which is associated with hantavirus research. The study emphasized the role of live animal trade in increasing pathogen exposure through multispecies aggregation and human-animal contact. It also noted that only 10.7% of participants recognized zoonotic transmission routes, underscoring the need for improved awareness. The findings support integrated One Health surveillance at wildlife trade interfaces and provide a pre-COVID baseline for future risk assessments. However, the study's focus on animal specimens and lack of human viral detection limit its scope, resulting in moderate evidence strength.
